parts.label: (a)
hints: Hint 1: Think about what a capacitor physically does - it holds separated charge on two plates. Where in everyday electronics is briefly holding charge or holding voltage steady useful?
Hint 2: Think of a second, quite different job - what happens to steady d.c. once a capacitor is fully charged, and where is a controlled charge-discharge time useful?
parts.proper_answer: 1. Store electrical energy / charge and release it when needed. 2. Smoothing of rectified a.c. to reduce ripple on d.c. supply (accept also: block d.c. while passing a.c., provide time delay / timing, produce oscillations, tuning of resonant circuits, prevent sparking).
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall what a capacitor is for**
Think of a capacitor as a tiny rechargeable store for charge. When connected to a supply it charges up, and later it can discharge quickly to deliver energy. That is why camera flashes, back-up supplies and many power circuits use them.

Step 2: **Find two distinct uses**
One family of uses is about energy and voltage: storing energy, or smoothing a bumpy rectified voltage to give steady d.c. A second family is about controlling signals and time: blocking steady d.c. but letting changing signals through, setting a time delay with a resistor, making oscillators or tuning radio circuits, and suppressing sparks across switch contacts. Any two different ones from this list earn the marks.

parts.label: (b)
hints: Hint 1: Look at Fig. 6.1 - the three capacitors are in one single loop with no junctions. What does charge conservation and electrostatic induction tell you about the magnitude of charge on each capacitor when plate P gets +q?
Hint 2: Think about voltages around the loop. How is the battery e.m.f. $E$ shared between the three p.d.s $V_1$, $V_2$, $V_3$, and how is each p.d. linked to charge and its own capacitance?
Hint 3: Write the combined capacitor as $E = q/C$ and substitute for $E$ and each $V$. What happens when you divide every term by the common charge $q$?
parts.proper_answer: Each capacitor in series carries the same charge $q$. $E = V_1+V_2+V_3$ with $V_1=q/C_1$, $V_2=q/C_2$, $V_3=q/C_3$ and $E=q/C$. Hence $q/C = q/C_1+q/C_2+q/C_3$, giving $1/C = 1/C_1+1/C_2+1/C_3$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Why the charge is the same**
When the switch closes, +q arrives on plate P from the battery. It attracts -q onto the opposite plate of $C_1$. That isolated conductor between $C_1$ and $C_2$ must stay neutral overall, so +q is pushed onto the next plate, and so on. You are sitting beside the circuit watching electrons shuffle along - every capacitor ends up with charge of magnitude $q$.

Step 2: **Share the e.m.f. between the capacitors**
Going round the loop, the sum of the p.d.s across the capacitors must equal the battery e.m.f.: $$E = V_1 + V_2 + V_3$$ For any capacitor, $$Q = CV \;\; \text{so} \;\; V = Q/C$$ Hence: $$V_1 = q/C_1, \; V_2 = q/C_2, \; V_3 = q/C_3$$

Step 3: **Introduce the combined capacitance**
Define the single equivalent capacitor $C$ that would store the same charge $q$ with the same e.m.f. $E$: $$E = q/C$$ Substitute into the voltage equation: $$q/C = q/C_1 + q/C_2 + q/C_3$$ Divide through by the common $q$: $$\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2} + \frac{1}{C_3}$$ That is the series rule.

parts.label: (c)(i)
hints: Hint 1: Remember parallel adds capacitance while series reduces it. Starting from $20\,\mu\text{F}$, do you need to add or reduce to reach $60\,\mu\text{F}$, and how many capacitors does that need?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Use parallel to increase capacitance**
In parallel each capacitor sees the same voltage, so total stored charge adds. That means capacitances simply add: $$C_{parallel} = C_1 + C_2 + C_3 + ...$$ Three $20\,\mu\text{F}$ side-by-side give $$C = 20 + 20 + 20 = 60\,\mu\text{F}$$ So draw three capacitor symbols with their ends joined to two common wires.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: $15\,\mu\text{F}$ is less than $20\,\mu\text{F}$, so you must use series somewhere, but a simple series of $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitors cannot give 15. Try making a larger block first with parallel, then put that block in series with the remaining capacitor.
parts.proper_answer: Connect three $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitors in parallel to give $60\,\mu\text{F}$, in series with the fourth $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor. $1/C = 1/60+1/20 = 1/15$, so $C = 15\,\mu\text{F}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Combine parallel then series**
First make a $60\,\mu\text{F}$ block as in (i) using three capacitors in parallel. Then put this block in series with the fourth $20\,\mu\text{F}$ capacitor. For the series step: $$\frac{1}{C} = \frac{1}{60} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{1+3}{60} = \frac{4}{60} = \frac{1}{15}$$ so $$C = 15\,\mu\text{F}$$ This uses all four capacitors to hit exactly the required value.
